passage.title: Carved by a Single Drop
passage.author: DRC BEACON Assessment Passage
passage.text:
Deep beneath grassy hills and forest floors, giant rooms of stone sit in total darkness. These underground halls are called limestone caves. No human builders ever swung a pickaxe or shovel to dig them out. Instead, plain rainwater did all the work over thousands of years. As rain falls through the sky and soaks into dead leaves on the ground, it picks up carbon dioxide gas. This gas turns the water into a weak acid that does not burn skin, though it can dissolve soft rock.

Drops of this weak acid seep down through thin cracks in the gray limestone. Year after year, the moving water eats away tiny bits of stone along each split. Thin cracks slowly grow into tunnels, and small tunnels join to form huge chambers. At first, groundwater fills the entire space from floor to ceiling. Later, when nearby rivers cut deeper into the valley, the water drains out and leaves an empty cave filled with air.

Once air fills the cave, the same dripping water begins to build new rock shapes instead of carving them away. Each drop that seeps through the cave roof carries dissolved mineral from the limestone above. When a drop hangs from the ceiling and meets the cave air, it loses a bit of gas. A tiny ring of solid mineral, left behind on the stone ceiling before the water falls, is slowly built up by thousands of drops into a hanging stalactite. It looks like a stone icicle pointing straight down.

The work of that single drop does not end when it lets go of the ceiling. The falling drop splashes onto the cave floor directly below the tip of the stalactite. There, it leaves one more tiny speck of mineral on the ground. Over centuries, these floor specks stack up to form a thick cone called a stalagmite. Cave guides tell the two apart by remembering that stalactites hold tight to the ceiling, while stalagmites might reach the roof.

At times, a hanging cone and a rising cone grow long enough to meet in the middle. When they fuse together, they form a solid stone pillar from floor to ceiling. Cave rocks grow so slowly that a single inch of new stone can take more than a hundred years to form. Because skin oils from human fingers stop mineral rings from sticking to the wet stone, park rangers ask visitors to never touch a cave wall.

tier2Words.definition: to melt or break down a solid substance into tiny invisible parts inside a liquid
tier2Words.contextClue: The weak acid does not burn skin, but it can break down soft limestone rock as it seeps through cracks.

tier2Words.definition: to flow or leak slowly through small openings or porous material
tier2Words.rootHint: From Old English sipian, meaning 'to soak or trickle slowly'
tier2Words.contextClue: Trickles of water leak slowly downward through narrow cracks in the gray limestone bedrock.

tier2Words.definition: large enclosed rooms or open spaces, especially underground
tier2Words.contextClue: Narrow cracks widen into tunnels, and small tunnels join to form huge underground rooms.

tier2Words.definition: to join or blend two separate things together into a single solid piece
tier2Words.rootHint: From Latin fundere, meaning 'to melt or pour together'
tier2Words.contextClue: When a hanging stalactite and a rising stalagmite meet in the middle and join together, they form a solid stone column.

questions.prompt:
Read this sentence from Paragraph 3:

"A tiny ring of solid mineral, left behind on the stone ceiling before the water falls, is slowly built up by thousands of drops into a hanging stalactite."

Based on the structure of the sentence, what builds the tiny ring of solid mineral into a hanging stalactite?

options.text: Park rangers build the mineral rings using special cave tools.
The stone ceiling builds thousands of water drops before they fall.
A hanging stalactite builds the stone ceiling out of rainwater.
Thousands of drops build the tiny ring of mineral into a stalactite.

questions.provingSentenceText: A tiny ring of solid mineral, left behind on the stone ceiling before the water falls, is slowly built up by thousands of drops into a hanging stalactite.
questions.childTip: Look for the 'by' phrase right after 'is slowly built up' to find what does the building.
questions.parentExplanation: In this passive-voice sentence, 'A tiny ring of solid mineral' receives the action, while the prepositional phrase 'by thousands of drops' identifies the agent that builds the stalactite.

questions.prompt:
Read these sentences from Paragraph 5:

"At times, a hanging cone and a rising cone grow long enough to meet in the middle. When they fuse together, they form a solid stone pillar from floor to ceiling."

What does the word fuse mean as it is used in Paragraph 5?

options.text: Crack apart into tiny grains of gray sand
Drip quickly from a high stone roof
Join and bond into one solid piece
Shine brightly in a dark underground room

questions.provingSentenceText: When they fuse together, they form a solid stone pillar from floor to ceiling.
questions.childTip: When the hanging and rising rock shapes meet in the middle, they join into one solid column.
questions.parentExplanation: Paragraph 5 explains that a stalactite and stalagmite grow until they meet in the middle and form a single solid stone pillar, showing that 'fuse' means to join or bond into one piece.

questions.prompt: According to Paragraph 1, how does plain rainwater gain the ability to dissolve solid limestone rock?

options.text: It heats up to a boiling temperature as it flows past deep underground rivers.
It picks up carbon dioxide gas from the air and dead leaves, turning into a weak acid.
It mixes with skin oils left behind by visitors walking on the forest floor.
It carries sharp pebbles that scrape the cave walls during heavy summer floods.

questions.provingSentenceText: As rain falls through the sky and soaks into dead leaves on the ground, it picks up carbon dioxide gas.
questions.childTip: Click the sentence in Paragraph 1 that tells what rainwater picks up as it falls and soaks into dead leaves.
questions.parentExplanation: Paragraph 1 states that rainwater picks up carbon dioxide gas from the sky and dead leaves on the ground, which turns the water into a weak acid capable of dissolving limestone.

questions.prompt: In Paragraph 5, why does the author explain the effect of human skin oils on wet stone?

options.text: To support the point that cave visitors should never touch cave formations
To prove that human skin is stronger than weakly acidic rainwater
To show how park rangers polish stalactites so they look like stone icicles
To argue that all underground caves should be closed to every scientist

questions.provingSentenceText: Because skin oils from human fingers stop mineral rings from sticking to the wet stone, park rangers ask visitors to never touch a cave wall.
questions.childTip: Read the last sentence of Paragraph 5 to see why park rangers ask visitors not to touch the rock.
questions.parentExplanation: In alignment with ELAGSE5RI8 (author's reasons and evidence), the author gives the scientific reason—skin oils prevent mineral rings from sticking—to support the rule that visitors must not touch cave walls.

questions.prompt: Part A: Which claim does the author make in Paragraph 3 about how water's role in a cave changes over time?

options.text: Once air enters a cave, rainwater loses all of its minerals and can no longer drip from the roof.
Once air fills an empty cave, dripping water switches from carving away rock to building new rock shapes.
Water can only form stalactites when the entire cave chamber is completely flooded from floor to ceiling.
Dripping water builds a full-sized stone pillar from floor to ceiling in less than one week.

questions.provingSentenceText: Once air fills the cave, the same dripping water begins to build new rock shapes instead of carving them away.
questions.childTip: Look at the first sentence of Paragraph 3 to see how dripping water changes its job once air fills the cave.
questions.parentExplanation: Paragraph 3 opens with the key claim that once water drains and air fills the cave, the dripping water shifts from dissolving/carving limestone to depositing calcite minerals that build new formations.

questions.prompt: Which quotation from the passage best supports the correct answer to Question 5?

options.text: "No human builders ever swung a pickaxe or shovel to dig them out."
"At first, groundwater fills the entire space from floor to ceiling."
"The falling drop splashes onto the cave floor directly below the tip of the stalactite."
"Once air fills the cave, the same dripping water begins to build new rock shapes instead of carving them away."

questions.provingSentenceText: Once air fills the cave, the same dripping water begins to build new rock shapes instead of carving them away.
questions.childTip: Pick the quote from Paragraph 3 that directly contrasts building new rock shapes with carving them away.
questions.parentExplanation: Option C is the exact sentence in Paragraph 3 that states how water transitions from carving rock to building new rock shapes once air fills the cave.
